81272529.title: 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election
81272529.extract:
The 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election was held on November 4, 2025, to determine whether 3 Pennsylvania Supreme Court justices would serve their second 10-year terms. Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht, who were first elected as Democrats in 2015, were all retained by large margins, including in over a dozen counties won by Donald Trump in 2024.


== Background ==
The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania currently has a 5-2 Democratic majority. The court has been Democratic-controlled since 2015, when Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht won election to their seats. 
Had voters chosen not to retain any of the justices, Governor Josh Shapiro could have appointed a temporary replacement until 2027 — with approval from two-thirds of the Republican-controlled Pennsylvania Senate — when an election would have been held for a permanent replacement. If all three justices were not retained and the Senate did not approve Shapiro's nominees, the court would be split with two Democrats and two Republicans, which The Philadelphia Inquirer claimed could leave the court "unlikely to reach majority decisions and could weaken the voice of Pennsylvania's top court going into the 2028 presidential election, when the swing state could decide the next president yet again."
Since retention elections were established in 1968, only one Pennsylvania justice, Russell Nigro in 2005, has not been retained.


== Campaign ==
The justices themselves were not permitted to directly campaign. Instead, they engaged in a statewide speaking tour where they pledged to exercise their judicial power without partisan bias. The Philadelphia Inquirer said that over $14 million had been raised in support of retention, while the Brennan Center for Justice estimated that $7.5 million has been spent by liberal political action committees on TV ads in support of a 'Yes' vote to "protect elections and preserve abortion rights". They also claimed that the race was the second most expensive retention election in U.S. history. 
Deborah Gross, executive director of the non-profit Pennsylvanians for Modern Courts, claimed that the significant spending 'perverts the intent of the retention process' by focusing on party affiliation rather than the justices' records. Talking to the Pennsylvania Capital-Star, Gross said, "[i]f someone is not doing their job properly, if they're not showing up for court, if they're doing bad acts, if they have judicial conduct issues. Those are reasons why someone should not be retained."
The Democratic National Committee announced a "six-figure investment" into the Pennsylvania Democratic Party to help support retaining the 3 judges, with DNC Chair Ken Martin issuing a statement saying that "[t]he Pennsylvania Supreme Court is on the frontlines of decisions related to voting rights, redistricting, abortion protections" and that "[t]he stakes couldn't be higher."
The state and national chapters of the ACLU spent $500,000 on a mail campaign to inform voters about the race "and what it means for their civil rights and civil liberties." The organization's website did not make an explicit case for or against retaining any of the judges.
Conservative activist Scott Presler told Fox News that his PAC, Early Vote Action, was targeting Bucks County — which voted Republican in 2024 for the first time in almost four decades — by sending 100,000 text messages as part of a campaign that recognizes Charlie Kirk’s birthday. Presler also stated that the group was producing stickers that say 'I voted in honor of Charlie' with a "really classy photo" of Kirk with his hands together in prayer. Bucks County chose to retain all 3 justices by over 20 points.
Multiple PACs affiliated with Republican businessman Matthew Brouillette and funded almost entirely by billionaire Jeff Yass — a registered Libertarian — spent millions on social media ads, mailers, and text messages opposing retaining all 3 judges, telling voters they should “term limit the woke Democrat Pennsylvania Supreme Court.” 


=== Mailer controversy ===
The Commonwealth Leaders Fund, a Yass-affiliated PAC, was criticized by the advocacy group Fair Districts PA after they sent out mailers claiming that the "liberal Supreme Court gerrymandered our congressional districts to help Democrats win." The mailers also featured an outdated image of 2 congressional districts from a map that was drawn up by the Republican-controlled state legislature in 2011 and later overturned for partisan gerrymandering that disproportionately benefitted the Republican Party.
After the mailer controversy was publicized, Pennsylvania Democratic Party chair Eugene DePasquale issued a statement condemning "MAGA billionaires" for funneling money into the election. In late September, 2025, the Pennsylvania Working Families Party organized a protest outside Susquehanna International Group, a financial trading company founded by Jeff Yass, criticizing his involvement in the campaign and urging passers-by to "Vote 'Yes', not Yass". 
The League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania declined to endorse for or against retention, though they criticized the leading 'No' campaign PACs for misleading voters by including inaccurate information on their campaign mailers. In 2017, the group argued in a lawsuit that Republican-gerrymandered maps violate the state constitution's guarantee of free and fair elections. The state Supreme Court, which included the 3 justices up for retention, ruled in favor of the claim.


== Election logistics ==
The voter registration deadline was set for October 20, 2025, two weeks before the election. With limited exceptions, ballots had to be received by 8pm on election day to be counted. Pennsylvania permits the use of mail-in ballots, including no-excuse postal votes, allowing any registered voter to request a mail-in ballot. However, state law prohibits pre-processing of received mail-in ballots, meaning election officials had to wait until election day to begin ballot curing.
Republican activists and politicians urged voters to cast mail-in ballots before election day, despite Donald Trump's repeated support for a ban on mail-in voting. The Pennsylvania Republican Party encouraged voters to request an absentee ballot, posting on Twitter that "if there is even a 1% chance that you might miss the 2025 Election, sign up for a mail-in ballot today! It's quick and easy!"
Increased Republican support for mail-in voting was also seen in the New Jersey gubernatorial election, where unsuccessful Republican candidate Jack Ciattarelli boasted that "more Republicans [have] return[ed] vote-by-mail ballots than ever before." Similarly, the California Republican Party urged the use of mail-in ballots to vote against Proposition 50, a ballot measure that permitted redrawing the state's congressional districts.
Despite all three justices originally running as Democrats, retention elections are considered nonpartisan, meaning that ballots do not feature a candidate's party affiliation. Votebeat spoke to a voter who expressed frustration over this, saying that they weren’t immediately sure if the justices were Republicans or Democrats. Chris Borick, a professor of political science at Muhlenberg College, told Votebeat that the removal of partisan designation on a retention ballot can confuse voters.


=== Chester County provisional ballots ===
On election day, NBC News reported that independent and unaffiliated voters in Chester County were forced to cast provisional ballots after poll books listing only Republicans and Democrats were delivered to polling sites, meaning that independent voters didn't appear as registered voters, and their ballots were only counted after election officials were able to prove their eligibility. A county spokeswoman later confirmed that voters registered as Libertarians or Greens were also forced to cast their votes with provisional ballots.
Chester County posted on social media that "supplemental poll books" were sent out to 230 polling sites, allowing voters to vote normally throughout the afternoon and evening. A judge later extended polling hours in the county until 10pm rather than 8pm to allow impacted voters to cast non-provisional ballots.
Two weeks after election day, Spotlight PA confirmed that roughly 11,200 of the 12,600 provisional ballots used in Chester County were counted in the final tally. The newspaper also reported that the Republican Committee of Chester County challenged around 1,400 provisional ballots, some of which were missing signatures from voters or poll workers. 
In a hearing on November 17, 2025, the Republican Committee dropped most of their objections, with the exception of ballots received in unsigned envelopes, and ballots that had no envelopes at all. The Chester County Board of Elections, who held the hearing, voted 2-1 to accept ballots where the voter had not signed the envelope in the correct place, as well as signed ballots that were received without envelopes. The board also voted unanimously to reject three unsigned ballots without envelopes. Some 300 other provisional ballots were rejected for other reasons, including a number of ballots filled out by unregistered voters.
That same day, Chester County officials announced they had hired a law firm to investigate the missing poll books. According to CBS News, investigators will interview county staff and examine current election processes prior to making their final recommendations for improvement at a public meeting scheduled to be held sometime in January 2026.


== Seat 2 ==


=== Background ===
Christine Donohue was first elected in 2015, and assumed office the year after. Prior to being elected, Donohue served on the Superior Court of Pennsylvania, as well as on the Pennsylvania Judicial Conduct Board and the Pennsylvania Court of Judicial Discipline. She also served as a member of the Pennsylvania Board of Law Examiners. Before that, she served as a civil trial lawyer and litigator for nearly three decades.
In 2024, Donohue voted with the majority to order lower courts to reconsider the legality of barring Medicaid recipients from receiving abortion services.

"The Pennsylvania Constitution secures the fundamental right to reproductive autonomy, which includes the right to decide whether to have an abortion or carry a pregnancy to term."

In 2022, Donohue wrote the majority opinion in the case which upheld Pennsylvania's no-excuse mail voting law. The law allows Pennsylvania voters to apply for mail-in ballots without providing a reason why they need to vote by mail. That same year, she sided with the majority in a case that determined Pennsylvania's school funding system was unconstitutional because it disadvantaged lower-income school districts.

{{Short description|none}}{{good article}} {{Use mdy dates|date=October 2025}} {{Infobox multichoice referendum | name = 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election | title = Shall Christine Donohue be retained for an additional term as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania? | country = Pennsylvania | date = November 4, 2025 | choice1 = Yes | percentage1 = 61.80 | choice2 = No | percentage2 = 38.20 }} {{Infobox multichoice referendum | name = | title = Shall Kevin M. Dougherty be retained for an additional term as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania? | country = | date = | choice1 = Yes | percentage1 = 61.79 | choice2 = No | percentage2 = 38.21 }} {{Infobox multichoice referendum | name = | title = Shall David Wecht be retained for an additional term as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania? | country = | date = | choice1 = Yes | percentage1 = 61.46 | choice2 = No | percentage2 = 38.54 }} {{ElectionsPA}} The '''2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election''' was held on November 4, 2025, to determine whether 3 [[Supreme Court of Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania Supreme Court]] justices would serve their second 10-year terms. [[Christine Donohue]], [[Kevin Dougherty]], and [[David Wecht]], who were first elected as [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] in [[2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election|2015]], were all retained by large margins, including in over a dozen counties{{efn| '''Retained all justices'''
*[[Erie County, Pennsylvania|Erie]] *[[Beaver County, Pennsylvania|Beaver]] *[[Washington County, Pennsylvania|Washington]] *[[Union County, Pennsylvania|Union]] *[[Montour County, Pennsylvania|Montour]] *[[Columbia County, Pennsylvania|Columbia]] *[[Luzerne County, Pennsylvania|Luzerne]] *[[Pike County, Pennsylvania|Pike]] *[[Monroe County, Pennsylvania|Monroe]] *[[Northampton County, Pennsylvania|Northampton]] *[[Bucks County, Pennsylvania|Bucks]] *[[Berks County, Pennsylvania|Berks]] *[[Lancaster County, Pennsylvania|Lancaster]] *[[Cumberland County, Pennsylvania|Cumberland]] *[[Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania|Westmoreland]] '''Retained Dougherty only'''
*[[Northumberland County, Pennsylvania|Northumberland]] '''Retained Dougherty and Donohue only'''
*[[York County, Pennsylvania|York]] }} won by [[Donald Trump]] in [[2024 United States presidential election|2024]].{{cite web |last1=Armstrong |first1=Gene |title=Pennsylvania Supreme Court election results {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://edition.cnn.com/election/2025/results/pennsylvania |website=CNN |access-date=5 November 2025 |language=en}} ==Background== The [[Supreme Court of Pennsylvania]] currently has a 5-2 Democratic majority.{{cite web |title=Democrats expand majority on PA Supreme Court |url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2023/11/07/election-day/democrats-pennsylvania-supreme-court-election-results-00126000 |website=POLITICO |language=en |date=8 November 2023}} The court has been [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]]-controlled since [[2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election|2015]], when [[Christine Donohue|Donohue]], [[Kevin Dougherty|Dougherty]], and [[David Wecht|Wecht]] won election to their seats.{{cite web |title=Voters Give Dems Control Of Pennsylvania Supreme Court |url=https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2015-11-03/voters-give-dems-control-of-pennsylvania-supreme-court |website=90.5 WESA from Associated Press |language=en |date=4 November 2015}} Had voters chosen not to retain any of the justices, [[List of governors of Pennsylvania|Governor]] [[Josh Shapiro]] could have appointed a temporary replacement until 2027 — with approval from two-thirds of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]]-controlled [[Pennsylvania State Senate|Pennsylvania Senate]]{{cite web |last1=Levine |first1=Sam |title=Pennsylvania keeps three liberal justices, preserving swing-state court control |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/nov/04/pennsylvania-supreme-court-election |website=The Guardian |access-date=27 November 2025 |date=5 November 2025}} — when an election would have been held for a permanent replacement.{{cite web |title=Republicans have a chance to transform the Pa. Supreme Court this year |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/02/judicial-retention-election-pennsylvania-2025-supreme-court-partisan/ |website=Spotlight}} If all three justices were not retained and the Senate did not approve Shapiro's nominees, the court would be split with two Democrats and two Republicans, which ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' claimed could leave the court "unlikely to reach majority decisions and could weaken the voice of Pennsylvania's top court going into the [[2028 United States presidential election|2028 presidential election]], when the [[swing state]] could decide the next president yet again."{{cite web |last1=McGoldrick |first1=Gillian |title=Republicans are attempting to boot three Democratic justices from the Pa. Supreme Court — and for the first time, Dems are worried |url=https://www.inquirer.com/news/pennsylvania/pennsylvania-supreme-court-justices-retention-election-20250511.html |website=Inquirer.com |language=en |date=11 May 2025}} Since [[retention election|retention elections]] were established in 1968, only one Pennsylvania justice, [[Russell M. Nigro|Russell Nigro]] in [[2005 Pennsylvania elections|2005]], has not been retained.{{cite web |title=DLCC Adds PA State Supreme Court Race to Target Map - PoliticsPA |url=https://www.politicspa.com/dlcc-adds-pa-state-supreme-court-race-to-target-map/140810/ |website=PoliticsPA |date=25 February 2025}} ==Campaign== The justices themselves were not permitted to directly campaign. Instead, they engaged in a statewide speaking tour where they pledged to exercise their judicial power without [[partisan bias]].{{cite web |title=Pennsylvania Supreme Court Election Sparks National Interest |url=https://www.multistate.us/insider/2025/10/17/pennsylvania-supreme-court-election-sparks-national-interest |website=MultiState |access-date=20 October 2025}} ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' said that over $14 million had been raised in support of retention,{{cite web |last1=Yerardi |first1=Joe Yerardi |last2=Bernard |first2=Katie |title=Democrats feared Republican efforts to oust Pa. Supreme Court justices. They spent significantly more on the race |url=https://kdhnews.com/news/politics/democrats-feared-republican-efforts-to-oust-pa-supreme-court-justices-they-spent-significantly-more-on/article_6cc1c08d-5ee7-5618-9d1c-d0edc5a02e7b.html |website=The Killeen Daily Herald |access-date=2 November 2025 |language=en |date=2 November 2025}} while the [[Brennan Center for Justice]] estimated that $7.5 million has been spent by liberal political action committees on TV ads in support of a 'Yes' vote to "protect elections and preserve abortion rights". They also claimed that the race was the second most expensive retention election in U.S. history.{{cite web |title=Fight over Pa. Supreme Court emerges as latest costly battle over abortion, election law |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/election-2025/2025/10/12/pennsylvania-supreme-court-abortion-election/stories/202510090096 |website=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |language=en}}{{cite web |last1=Shortell |first1=Tom |title=Election 2025: Why Pa. Supreme Court retention questions have taken center stage |url=https://www.lehighvalleynews.com/elections/election-2025-why-pa-supreme-court-retention-questions-have-taken-center-stage |website=Lehigh Valley News |access-date=2 November 2025 |language=en |date=1 November 2025}} Deborah Gross, executive director of the non-profit Pennsylvanians for Modern Courts, claimed that the significant spending 'perverts the intent of the retention process' by focusing on party affiliation rather than the justices' records. Talking to the ''[[Pennsylvania Capital-Star]]'', Gross said, "[i]f someone is not doing their job properly, if they're not showing up for court, if they're doing bad acts, if they have judicial conduct issues. Those are reasons why someone should not be retained."{{cite web |last1=Hall |first1=Peter |title=Voting rights group calls on conservative PAC to renounce misleading Supreme Court mailers • Pennsylvania Capital-Star |url=https://penncapital-star.com/government-politics/voting-rights-group-calls-on-conservative-pac-to-renounce-misleading-supreme-court-mailers/ |website=Pennsylvania Capital-Star |date=14 October 2025}} The [[Democratic National Committee]] announced a "six-figure investment" into the [[Pennsylvania Democratic Party]] to help support retaining the 3 judges,{{cite web |last1=Reese |first1=Shelby |title=DNC Announces Initial Six-Figure Investment in Pennsylvania Democratic Party Ahead of Critical Election to Retain PA Supreme Court Justices |url=https://democrats.org/news/dnc-announces-initial-six-figure-investment-in-pennsylvania-democratic-party-ahead-of-critical-election-to-retain-pa-supreme-court-justices/ |website=Democratic Party |language=en |date=25 September 2025}} with [[List of chairs of the Democratic National Committee|DNC Chair]] [[Ken Martin]] issuing a statement saying that "[t]he Pennsylvania Supreme Court is on the frontlines of decisions related to voting rights, redistricting, abortion protections" and that "[t]he stakes couldn't be higher." The state and national chapters of the [[American Civil Liberties Union|ACLU]] spent $500,000 on a mail campaign to inform voters about the race "and what it means for their civil rights and civil liberties." The organization's website did not make an explicit case for or against retaining any of the judges.{{cite web |title=ACLU and ACLU of PA Launch $500K Campaign to Raise Awareness About State Supreme Court Retention Election |url=https://www.aclupa.org/press-releases/aclu-and-aclu-of-pa-launch-500k-campaign-to-raise-awareness-about-state-supreme-court-retention-election/ |website=ACLU of Pennsylvania |access-date=27 November 2025}} Conservative activist [[Scott Presler]] told ''[[Fox News]]'' that his [[political action committee|PAC]], Early Vote Action, was targeting [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania|Bucks County]] — which voted [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] in [[2024 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2024]] for the first time in almost [[1988 United States presidential election|four decades]] — by sending 100,000 text messages as part of a campaign that recognizes [[Charlie Kirk]]’s birthday. Presler also stated that the group was producing stickers that say 'I voted in honor of Charlie' with a "really classy photo" of Kirk with his hands together in prayer.{{cite web |last1=Oliver |first1=Ashley |title=Republicans mount campaign to flip Pennsylvania Supreme Court's Democratic majority |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/republicans-mount-campaign-flip-pennsylvania-supreme-courts-democratic-majority |website=Fox News |date=13 October 2025}} Bucks County chose to retain all 3 justices by over 20 points. Multiple PACs affiliated with Republican businessman [[Matthew Brouillette]] and funded almost entirely by billionaire [[Jeff Yass]] — a registered [[Libertarian Party of Pennsylvania|Libertarian]] — spent millions on social media ads, mailers, and text messages opposing retaining all 3 judges, telling voters they should “term limit the woke Democrat Pennsylvania Supreme Court.”{{cite web |last1=Meyer |first1=Katie |title=PA Supreme Court mailer uses misleading redistricting claims |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-misleading-redistricting-claims-elections/ |website=Spotlight PA |language=en-us |date=30 September 2025}}{{cite web |last1=Kalra |first1=Avani |title=This Republican Mega-Donor Is Changing Local Elections In Pennsylvania |url=https://www.notus.org/pennsylvania/jeffrey-yass-elections-supreme-court |website=NOTUS |access-date=27 November 2025 |date=3 November 2025 |quote=Yass-funded groups are now pouring millions into the state’s Supreme Court retention race taking place on Tuesday, a typically low-key race in which incumbent candidates run without a party affiliation.}} ===Mailer controversy=== The Commonwealth Leaders Fund, a Yass-affiliated PAC, was criticized by the advocacy group Fair Districts PA after they sent out mailers claiming that the "liberal Supreme Court gerrymandered our congressional districts to help Democrats win." The mailers also featured an outdated image of 2 [[Pennsylvania House of Representatives|congressional districts]] from a map that was drawn up by the Republican-controlled [[Pennsylvania General Assembly|state legislature]] in 2011 and later overturned for partisan [[gerrymandering]] that disproportionately benefitted the Republican Party.{{cite web |last1=Caruso |first1=Stephen |title=A national Democratic group, the ACLU, and Pa.'s richest person are spending on judicial retention |url=https://www.wesa.fm/politics-government/2025-10-01/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-spending-aclu-jeff-yass |website=90.5 WESA |language=en |date=1 October 2025}} After the mailer controversy was publicized, [[Pennsylvania Democratic Party]] chair [[Eugene DePasquale]] issued a statement condemning "MAGA billionaires" for funneling money into the election.{{cite web |title=Pa. Democrats decry Jeffrey Yass spending in judicial races, compare him to Elon Musk |url=https://whyy.org/articles/pa-elections-democrats-jeffrey-yass-spending-judicial/ |website=WHYY}} In late September, 2025, the [[Working Families Party|Pennsylvania Working Families Party]] organized a protest outside [[Susquehanna International Group]], a financial trading company founded by [[Jeff Yass]], criticizing his involvement in the campaign and urging passers-by to "Vote 'Yes', not Yass". The [[League of Women Voters|League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania]] declined to endorse for or against retention, though they criticized the leading 'No' campaign PACs for misleading voters by including inaccurate information on their campaign mailers.{{cite web |title=“LWVPA Denounces Billionaire-Funded Disinformation Campaign Targeting Supreme Court Retention Election” (Via PoliticsPA) |url=https://www.palwv.org/news/lwvpa-denounces-billionaire-funded-disinformation-campaign-targeting-supreme-court-retention-election-via-politicspa |website=League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania}} In 2017, the group argued in a [[League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania v. Commonwealth of Pennsylvania|lawsuit]] that Republican-gerrymandered maps violate the [[Pennsylvania Constitution|state constitution]]'s guarantee of free and fair elections. The state Supreme Court, which included the 3 justices up for retention, ruled in favor of the claim. ==Election logistics== The voter registration deadline was set for October 20, 2025, two weeks before the election.{{cite web |title=2025 States to Watch: Pennsylvania |url=https://afjactioncampaign.org/state-courts-hub/2025-states-to-watch-pennsylvania/ |website=Alliance for Justice Action |access-date=27 November 2025 |language=en}} With limited exceptions, ballots had to be received by 8pm on election day to be counted.{{cite web |last1=Modi |first1=Ishani |title=Down the ballot: A voter’s guide to the 2025 Pennsylvania elections |url=https://www.thedp.com/article/2025/10/penn-pennsylvania-voter-guide-elections-2025/ |website=The Daily Pennsylvanian |access-date=27 November 2025}} [[Pennsylvania]] permits the use of [[Postal voting in the United States|mail-in ballots]], including [[Postal voting in the United States#No-excuse postal voting|no-excuse postal votes]], allowing any registered voter to request a mail-in ballot.{{cite web |title=Table 1: States with No-Excuse Absentee Voting |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/table-1-states-with-no-excuse-absentee-voting |website=National Conference of State Legislatures |access-date=27 November 2025}} However, state law prohibits [[Postal voting in the United States#Pre-processing of mail-in ballots|pre-processing]] of received mail-in ballots, meaning election officials had to wait until election day to begin [[ballot curing]].{{cite web |title=Data Dive: Timelines for Pre-Processing Mail Ballots |url=https://electioninnovation.org/research/data-dive-pre-processing-mail-ballots/ |website=The Center for Election Innovation & Research |access-date=27 November 2025}} Republican activists and politicians urged voters to cast mail-in ballots before election day, despite [[Donald Trump]]'s repeated support for a ban on mail-in voting.{{cite web |title=Republicans encourage voters to cast mail ballots, despite Trump's attacks |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/republicans-encourage-voters-cast-mail-ballots-despite-trumps/story?id=126909397 |website=ABC News |access-date=4 November 2025 |language=en}} The [[Pennsylvania Republican Party]] encouraged voters to request an [[absentee ballot]], posting on [[Twitter]] that "if there is even a 1% chance that you might miss the 2025 Election, sign up for a mail-in ballot today! It's quick and easy!" Increased Republican support for mail-in voting was also seen in the [[2025 New Jersey gubernatorial election|New Jersey gubernatorial election]], where unsuccessful Republican candidate [[Jack Ciattarelli]] boasted that "more Republicans [have] return[ed] vote-by-mail ballots than ever before."{{cite web |title=New Jersey gubernatorial candidates tout early voting numbers as Trump looms over tight race |url=https://www.aol.com/articles/jersey-gubernatorial-candidates-tout-early-110046317.html |website=AOL |access-date=4 November 2025 |date=30 October 2025}} Similarly, the [[California Republican Party]] urged the use of mail-in ballots to vote against [[2025 California Proposition 50|Proposition 50]], a ballot measure that permitted redrawing the state's congressional districts. Despite all three justices [[2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election|originally running]] as Democrats, retention elections are considered [[Non-partisan democracy|nonpartisan]], meaning that ballots do not feature a candidate's party affiliation.{{cite web |title=Election 2025: What is Judicial Retention, and Why Does it Matter for PA's Supreme Court Balance? |url=https://wjffradio.org/election-2025-what-is-judicial-retention-and-why-does-it-matter-for-pas-supreme-court-balance/ |website=WJFF Radio Catskill |access-date=27 November 2025 |date=18 September 2025}} ''[[Votebeat]]'' spoke to a voter who expressed frustration over this, saying that they weren’t immediately sure if the justices were Republicans or Democrats. [[Chris Borick]], a professor of political science at [[Muhlenberg College]], told ''Votebeat'' that the removal of partisan designation on a retention ballot can confuse voters.{{cite web |last1=Walker |first1=Carter |title=What PA voters said about judicial retention on Election Day |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/11/judicial-retention-pennsylvania-2025-election-voters-elections/ |website=[[Votebeat]] for [[Spotlight PA]] |access-date=27 November 2025 |language=en-us |date=4 November 2025}} ===Chester County provisional ballots=== On election day, ''[[NBC News]]'' reported that [[Independent voter|independent]] and unaffiliated voters in [[Chester County, Pennsylvania|Chester County]] were forced to cast [[Provisional ballot|provisional ballots]] after [[poll books]] listing only Republicans and Democrats were delivered to polling sites, meaning that independent voters didn't appear as registered voters, and their ballots were only counted after election officials were able to prove their eligibility.{{cite web |title=Chester County, PA pollbook error forces provisional voting |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/11/chester-county-pennsylvania-pollbook-error-provisional-ballots-elections/ |website=Spotlight PA |access-date=4 November 2025 |language=en-us |date=4 November 2025}} A county spokeswoman later confirmed that voters registered as [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarians]] or [[Green Party of the United States|Greens]] were also forced to cast their votes with provisional ballots. Chester County posted on social media that "supplemental poll books" were sent out to 230 polling sites, allowing voters to vote normally throughout the afternoon and evening.{{cite web |title=Pennsylvania county error leaves some voting provisionally |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/live-blog/election-day-2025-nyc-mayor-governor-race-live-updates-rcna241592/rcrd92521?canonicalCard=true |website=NBC News |access-date=4 November 2025 |language=en |date=4 November 2025}} A judge later extended polling hours in the county until 10pm rather than 8pm to allow impacted voters to cast non-provisional ballots.{{cite web |title=Voting extended until 10 p.m. in Chester Co. after third-party voters initially left off poll books |url=https://6abc.com/post/voting-issues-reported-chester-county-poll-books-missing-3rd-party-voters/18112177/ |website=6abc Philadelphia |access-date=5 November 2025 |language=en |date=4 November 2025}} Two weeks after election day, ''[[Spotlight PA]]'' confirmed that roughly 11,200 of the 12,600 provisional ballots used in Chester County were counted in the final tally.{{cite web |last1=Walker |first1=Carter |title=Chester County accepts vast majority of provisional ballots |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/11/chester-county-pennsylvania-accept-pollbook-provisional-ballot-problem-2025-election-elections/ |website=[[Spotlight PA]] |access-date=27 November 2025 |language=en-us |date=18 November 2025}} The newspaper also reported that the Republican Committee of Chester County challenged around 1,400 provisional ballots, some of which were missing signatures from voters or poll workers.{{cite web |last1=Samuel |first1=Jen |title=Chester County hires firm for independent investigation of election gaffe |url=https://www.dailylocal.com/2025/11/17/voters-ask-that-ballots-count-in-chester-county-during-public-hearing/ |website=Daily Local |access-date=27 November 2025 |date=17 November 2025}} In a hearing on November 17, 2025, the Republican Committee dropped most of their objections, with the exception of ballots received in unsigned envelopes, and ballots that had no envelopes at all. The Chester County [[Board of Elections]], who held the hearing, voted 2-1 to accept ballots where the voter had not signed the envelope in the correct place, as well as signed ballots that were received without envelopes. The board also voted unanimously to reject three unsigned ballots without envelopes. Some 300 other provisional ballots were rejected for other reasons, including a number of ballots filled out by unregistered voters. That same day, Chester County officials announced they had hired a law firm to investigate the missing poll books.{{cite web |title=An investigation is underway into Chester County’s Election Day poll book error |url=https://whyy.org/articles/chester-county-poll-book-investigation/ |website=WHYY |access-date=27 November 2025}} According to ''[[CBS News]]'', investigators will interview county staff and examine current election processes prior to making their final recommendations for improvement at a public meeting scheduled to be held sometime in January 2026.{{cite web |title=Chester County, Pennsylvania, hires law firm to investigate Election Day poll book issues - CBS Philadelphia |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/philadelphia/news/chester-county-pennsylvania-investigation-election-poll-book/ |website=CBS News |access-date=27 November 2025 |date=17 November 2025}} ==Seat 2== {{infobox referendum |name=2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court
Seat 2 retention election |date=November 4, 2025 |country= |title=Shall Christine Donohue be retained for an additional term as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania? |yes= 2,231,527 |no= 1,379,599 |invalid= |total= 3,611,126 |electorate= |map=Christine Donohue results by county.svg |map_caption='''Results by county''' {{col-begin}} {{col-2}} '''Yes''' {{legend|#28497C|80–90% |border=1px #AAAAAA solid}} {{legend|#47729E|70–80% |border=1px #AAAAAA solid}} {{legend|#7D9CBB|60–70% |border=1px #AAAAAA solid}} {{legend|#B6C8D9|50–60% |border=1px #AAAAAA solid}} {{col-2}} '''No''' {{legend|#8B8B54|70–80% |border=1px #AAAAAA solid}} {{legend|#BCBC83|60–70% |border=1px #AAAAAA solid}} {{legend|#DEDEBD|50–60% |border=1px #AAAAAA solid}} {{col-end}} }}{{nowrap|}} ===Background=== [[Christine Donohue]] was first elected in [[2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election|2015]], and assumed office the year after. Prior to being elected, Donohue served on the [[Superior Court of Pennsylvania]], as well as on the Pennsylvania Judicial Conduct Board and the Pennsylvania Court of Judicial Discipline. She also served as a member of the Pennsylvania Board of Law Examiners. Before that, she served as a [[civil trial]] lawyer and litigator for nearly three decades.{{cite web |last1=Soisson |first1=Isabel |title=Who's running for retention on the PA Supreme Court? |url=https://www.fox29.com/election/whos-running-retention-pa-supreme-court |website=FOX 29 Philadelphia |access-date=2 November 2025 |date=29 October 2025}} In 2024, Donohue voted with the majority to order lower courts to reconsider the legality of barring [[Medicaid]] recipients from receiving [[abortion]] services.{{cite web |title=Pennsylvania high court revives a case challenging Medicaid limits for abortions |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/01/29/1227704077/pennsylvania-supreme-court-case-challenging-medicaid-coverage-limits-abortion |website=NPR |access-date=2 November 2025 |language=en |date=29 January 2024}} {{Blockquote |text="''The [[Pennsylvania Constitution]] secures the [[Fundamental rights|fundamental right]] to reproductive autonomy, which includes the right to decide whether to have an abortion or carry a pregnancy to term.''" |author=Justice Christine Donohue }} In 2022, Donohue wrote the majority opinion in the case which upheld Pennsylvania's [[Postal voting in the United States|no-excuse mail voting]] law. The law allows Pennsylvania voters to apply for mail-in ballots without providing a reason why they need to vote by mail. That same year, she sided with the majority in [[William Penn School District v. Pennsylvania Department of Education|a case that determined Pennsylvania's school funding system was unconstitutional]] because it disadvantaged lower-income school districts.{{cite web |title=Case Spotlight: William Penn School District et al. v. Pennsylvania Department of Education et al. Summary |url=https://www.law.upenn.edu/live/files/12611-william-penn-summary-of-opinion-for-non-lawyerspdf |website=University of Pennsylvania |access-date=2 November 2025}} ===Endorsements=== {{endorsements box |title=''Support retention'' |colwidth=60 |list= ;Executive branch officials *[[Barack Obama]], former [[President of the United States]] (2009–2017){{cite web |title=President Donald Trump pushes for ‘no’ vote on Pa. Supreme Court retention election |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/election-2025/2025/11/03/donald-trump-pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election/stories/202511030034 |website=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |access-date=4 November 2025 |language=en |quote=Former President Barack Obama also spoke out last week about the Pennsylvania elections, urging voters to retain justices who “will protect your fundamental rights and freedoms.”}} *[[Eric Holder]], former [[United States Attorney General]] (2009–2015){{cite web |title=Endorsements - Pennsylvania Supreme Court elections, 2025 |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Pennsylvania_Supreme_Court_elections,_2025|website=Ballotpedia}} ;U.S. senators *[[John Fetterman]], [[Pennsylvania]] (2023–present) *[[Elissa Slotkin]], [[Michigan]] (2025–present){{cite web |title=A look at elections for downballot state offices in 2025 – Ballotpedia News |url=https://news.ballotpedia.org/2025/10/28/a-look-at-elections-for-downballot-state-offices-in-2025-2/ |website=Ballotpedia |access-date=29 October 2025 |date=28 October 2025}} ;U.S. representatives *[[Chris Deluzio]], [[Pennsylvania's 17th congressional district|PA-17]] (2023–present) ;Statewide officials *[[Josh Shapiro]], [[List of governors of Pennsylvania|governor]] of [[Pennsylvania]] (2023–present){{cite web |title=These Pennsylvania court races are usually sleepy. {{Legend|#e27f90ff|Trump, against retaining all}}{{Legend|#86b6f2ff|Harris, for retaining all}}{{Legend|#3aba52ff|Trump, for retaining all}}{{Legend|#85d994ff|Trump, for retaining Donohue and Dougherty}}{{Legend|#b5e1beff|Trump, for retaining Dougherty}}]] The justices were retained by large margins, with over 60% of the votes on all three ballot questions being in favor of retention. Fifteen counties{{efn| *[[Erie County, Pennsylvania|Erie]] *[[Beaver County, Pennsylvania|Beaver]] *[[Washington County, Pennsylvania|Washington]] *[[Union County, Pennsylvania|Union]] *[[Montour County, Pennsylvania|Montour]] *[[Columbia County, Pennsylvania|Columbia]] *[[Luzerne County, Pennsylvania|Luzerne]] *[[Pike County, Pennsylvania|Pike]] *[[Monroe County, Pennsylvania|Monroe]] *[[Northampton County, Pennsylvania|Northampton]] *[[Bucks County, Pennsylvania|Bucks]] *[[Berks County, Pennsylvania|Berks]] *[[Lancaster County, Pennsylvania|Lancaster]] *[[Cumberland County, Pennsylvania|Cumberland]] *[[Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania|Westmoreland]] }} that voted for [[Donald Trump]] in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2024 presidential election]] chose to retain all three justices.{{cite web |last1=McGoldrick |first1=Gillian |last2=Williams |first2=Chris |title=How 3 Pa. Supreme Court justices won retention — and why the process might never be the same |url=https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/supreme-court-retention-support-counties-20251107.html |website=The Philadelphia Inquirer |access-date=27 November 2025 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20251107114521/https://www.inquirer.com/politics/pennsylvania/supreme-court-retention-support-counties-20251107.html |archive-date=November 7, 2025 |language=en |date=7 November 2025}} Anti-retention campaigners heavily targeted [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania|Bucks County]], which the Democrats had carried for 8 consecutive elections before it was won by Trump in 2024 by less than three hundred votes.{{cite web |title=Pennsylvania election results 2024 {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://edition.cnn.com/election/2024/results/pennsylvania |website=CNN |access-date=27 November 2025 |language=en}} The county voted to retain each of the justices with margins of over 20 points. In [[Northumberland County, Pennsylvania|Northumberland County]], which Trump carried by 40 points in 2024, voters chose to retain only one justice, [[Kevin Dougherty]]. In [[York County, Pennsylvania|York County]], another Republican stronghold, voters chose to retain both Dougherty and [[Christine Donohue]]. In [[Union County, Pennsylvania|Union County]], where a Democratic candidate has not been backed at the presidential level since [[1832 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|1832]], all three justices were retained by an average of approximately 8%.{{Cite web|url=https://staffweb.wilkes.edu/harold.cox/pres/PaPres1832.html|title=Pennsylvania Presidential Election Returns 1832|access-date=27 November 2025}} Though [[Northeastern Pennsylvania]] has reliably voted Republican on the presidential level for decades, the three justices outperformed [[Kamala Harris]] in counties like [[Luzerne County, Pennsylvania|Luzerne]] and [[Montour County, Pennsylvania|Montour]], both of which chose to retain the three justices on 10 point margins despite Trump carrying them by 20 points. [[Chris Borick]], director of the [[Muhlenberg College Institute of Public Opinion]], told ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' that Democratic or independent voters upset with the [[Second Trump administration|Trump administration]] were more motivated to vote than they previously were, while Republican voters had a lower turnout compared to 2024. ==Aftermath== ===Reactions=== Despite the heavy spending, many voters reported that they had seen little political messaging leading up to the election. Speaking to ''[[Votebeat]]'', some voters in favor of retention said they wanted to send a message to [[Donald Trump]] when casting their ballots, though few voters claimed to be familiar with the justices' specific rulings. A representative from One Pennsylvania, a progressive non-profit, said the vote was a rejection of [[Jeff Yass]] and "the MAGA agenda." After the election was called, Justice Donohue released a statement saying that the result shows that "Pennsylvanians have trust in the independence of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court and, additionally, appreciate the importance of a stable Pennsylvania Supreme Court."{{cite web |last1=Levy |first1=Marc |title=Pennsylvania reelects Supreme Court justices, extending a Democratic majority
